_source: A Data Analytic Evaluation of Singapore Mahjong, Chapter 2 (rules) and Section 2.6 (variation survey).

turn_order.direction: counterclockwise, which from a seated player is to their RIGHT
turn_order._note: The player to your RIGHT plays after you. East (Banker) has the first turn.
turn_order.right_opponent: the player immediately after you; the ONLY opponent who may Chow your discard
turn_order.left_opponent: the player immediately before you; you may Chow THEIR discards
turn_order.engine_warning: Handedness is the opposite of Japanese convention. Verify seat direction in code rather than porting any seat-name-based heuristic.

mahjong.definition: One Eye plus four sets (Chow, Pong or Kong)
mahjong.eye_constraint: The Eye must be formed from Concealed Tiles only

kongs.kong_4: Four matching tiles declared from Concealed Tiles
kongs.kong_3: Claiming a Discarded Tile to extend three matching Concealed Tiles
kongs.kong_1: Adding a drawn tile to an already Exposed Pong
kongs.robbing: Permitted on Kong-1. Also permitted on Kong-4, but only for a 13 Wonders win.

tie_break: nearest player counterclockwise (to the right) of the discarder

prohibited_discard_use._note: Singapore's analogue of a temporary furiten. Contradicts the common claim that Singapore has no such rule.
rules: You may not claim a Discarded Tile identical to your own most recent discard.
You may not claim (for Pong or to Win) a Discarded Tile identical to any tile discarded by anyone AFTER your own last discard.
prohibited_discard_use.character: rolling - it clears once you discard again, unlike Riichi's permanent furiten

unplayable_tiles.meaning: The last 15 tiles of the wall cannot be drawn and yield no replacement tiles.

all_chow_restrictions: The Eye may not be a Dragon, the Player's Wind, or the Prevailing Wind.
Winning with only two Concealed Tiles cannot be All-Chow.
Winning on a Discarded Tile requires that you needed two or more unique tiles to win. This restriction does not apply to a Self-Draw.

pay_all._note: The 'Offending Player' pays every opponent's share. Structurally unlike anything in Japanese mahjong: one discard can carry three players' liability.

scenarios.desc: Discarding a Dragon, Prevailing Wind or Player's Wind that an opponent Pongs/Kongs, bringing their exposed Fan to the Fan Limit, and they then win.
scenarios.note: Each player may hold only ONE such infraction against them at a time; a later one replaces the earlier. All infractions clear at end of game.

scenarios.desc: Opponent has 3-4 Exposed Sets all in one suit or all Honors, and you discard the winning tile.
Opponent has two Dragon sets exposed and you discard the third.
Opponent has three Wind sets exposed and you discard the fourth.
Opponent has 3-4 Exposed Sets all Terminals and you discard the winning tile.
Discarding a Fresh Tile (one not already in the Discarded Tile Area) when fewer than 4 valid tiles remain, and it wins.
Discarding a Fresh Tile with fewer than 7 valid tiles remaining that causes a Kong-3; additional liability if they win on the replacement.

house_variations._note: Percentages are from the source's survey of real tables. Everything here should be config, not constants.

items.desc: Immediate payout for an Animal Pair or Flower Pair
Number of unplayable tiles at the wall's end
Immediate Kong payout values vary by table
Some tables award +1 Fan for a fully concealed Self-Draw win
Some tables award +1 Fan for any Self-Draw

items.fresh_definition_split: 50% count exposed tiles, 50% count discards only

items.desc: Fan for winning on the last valid tile
Whether a discard is required after the last valid tile
items.of_the_rest: 50% allow that discard to win; 40% forbid a Kong after the last valid tile

items.desc: Some tables require Pay All conditions to be announced aloud
Some tables recognise a Hong Kong style seven-pairs hand

digital_implementation_note: Sections 2.4 and 2.5 of the source cover table etiquette and remedies for irregular play - misdeals, exposed tiles, incorrect declarations, wrong tile counts. The source states these cannot occur in a computer implementation. Skip them; they are the largest block of rules text with the least relevance to a digital game.
